 PS6 RAM and Storage Alone Reportedly Cost Sony Over $680, Claims Leaker 
 by DrUsmanSaleem 
 Saturday, 16:33
 Discuss (43 Comments) 
 The memory crunch looks like it is hitting the PlayStation 6 harder than expected. Hardware leaker KeplerL2 claims on NeoGAF that the RAM and NAND flash storage in Sony's next console alone cost over $680. He posted it as a reply to a forum member who floated $680 as a possible subsidized retail price, which pretty much puts that idea to rest. Keep in mind that figure covers only memory and storage, before the APU, cooling, power supply, and the rest of the hardware are counted. This is not the first time Kepler has updated his estimate. Back in March, he put the console's bill of materials at around $760, and by July, that had climbed to roughly $960 . 
Current leaks suggest the PS6 uses GDDR7 memory on a 160-bit bus with support for up to 40 GB , with 30 GB considered the more likely configuration. There have also been reports that Sony looked into cutting memory capacity to keep costs down, and the culprit is the same as everywhere else: AI data centers are soaking up DRAM and NAND supply, which pushes prices up for everyone. Sony has said nothing official about PS6 pricing, so it's reasonable to treat all of this with some caution. That said, if memory prices stay where they are , a PS6 that costs significantly more than the PS5 Pro seems likely, and a $1,000 price tag now looks quite possible.

 I apologize for my long rant upfront, but this article hit my sore spot on a philosophical level.
I love how we're discussing hypotheticals about a hypothetical PS6 and its hypothetical $680 memory and storage costs while, in my opinion, much of the collective West is facing a very real economic, industrial and potentially existential crisis. Seriously, guys, I see two things here that I consider borderline pathological.
 First, do we even need a PS6 at this time (or a near-future time frame)? 
I'm not convinced we need or are getting besides a paper launch another console generation within the next five years, or perhaps even the next decade. The hardware development paradigm has shifted considerably. The same applies to GPUs, memory, storage and gaming hardware in general. Generational improvements are becoming prohibitively expensive, while the practical benefits don't justify the enormous resources required.
And I'm sorry to say this on a computer hardware forum of all places, but perhaps we should temporarily stop obsessing over the next piece of silicon and focus on something considerably more important and that is our economic and industrial survival. We should be squeezing substantially more out of the hardware we already have through software development, optimisation and better utilisation of existing resources. We don't have unlimited time, electricity, energy infrastructure, manufacturing capacity, raw materials or access to critical components anymore. And pretending otherwise won't magically manufacture another million GPUs for us gamers. They all go to military/Ai atm anyways .
 Second, I think we're seriously underestimating how fragile our entire technological supply chain has become. 
I'm not Michael Pachter with a crystal ball 🔮, and I'm certainly not claiming to know exactly what will happen. But whether we're discussing an RTX 6090, RTX 8090, PS6 or the next Xbox, I genuinely question whether these products will be available in anything resembling the quantities and at the prices we've grown accustomed to over the past decade. We're already dealing with extraordinary pricing pressures, geopolitical fragmentation, energy constraints and increasingly complicated global supply chains. These problems cannot necessarily be resolved by flipping a switch. 
Even if international trade and economic relations somehow returned to their pre2019 conditions tomorrow, rebuilding disrupted supply chains, industrial capacity and strategic reserves could still take years. Potentially many years. I'm genuinely concerned that the next decade will be defined less by exciting generational upgrades and more by availability, affordability, repairability and making existing hardware last considerably longer. Perhaps I'm being overly pessimistic. I sincerely hope so. But that brings me back to these articles. We're speculating about the hypothetical manufacturing costs of hypothetical hardware in a future market whose conditions we cannot meaningfully predict. That's speculation built on speculation built on speculation.
 I see it as a clickbait, nothing more, nothing less. 
I would much rather see manufacturers invest their resources into software optimisation, extending hardware lifespans and improving what we already own, rather than endlessly pushing another generation of increasingly expensive products into an increasingly uncertain market. We already have tremendous hardware and thousands of games worth playing. Nobody needs an RTX 8090 or a PS6 to enjoy gaming.
And yes, I realise how ridiculous it sounds to suggest slowing down hardware development on TechPowerUp, especially coming from someone who loves enthusiast hardware as much as I do 😅 But priorities matter. At this point we find ourselves in, we might have to accept that the next great technological achievement isn't necessarily building something faster.
It might simply be learning how to keep what we've already built running. Sorry for my long rant once more, I just got provoked by this article like a prawn (pun intended).
P.S.: Just a little reality check for all of us guys. The RTX 5090 that's suppose to cost 1999USD, I never gotten to buy practically below 3000e, now costs 8000 - 12000 euros. I meam come on. Give it a break System!
